name: Smilepill

card.summary: A looksmaxxing theory that a wide, warm, well-aligned smile can lift overall attractiveness enough to offset other facial traits.
card.note: Community opinion is split on whether smiling helps men's photos and first impressions.

quick.overview:
The smilepill is a term from looksmaxxing forums for the idea that a good smile can raise how attractive a face reads, sometimes enough to outweigh weaker features elsewhere. Proponents point to how many teeth show, how wide the smile is and how it frames the face.

The payoff is practical: if the theory holds for a person, working on the smile (dental alignment, palate width, whitening, expression) is a route to looking better. Discussion on looksmax.org is mostly anecdote and photo-rating results; no formal studies of the 'smilepill' itself are listed.
quick.how: Users discuss practising smiles in a mirror, posting smiling and neutral photos to rating sites for comparison, and dental or orthodontic changes such as palate expansion or alignment to change how much of the teeth show. Others argue the opposite and keep a neutral or slight-smirk expression in photos.
quick.risks: The theory itself carries no physical risk, but some of the associated routes (orthodontics, palate expansion, veneers) are dental procedures with their own risks and costs. Forum members disagree about whether smiling helps men, and some report it did not help them.

lead: The smilepill is looksmaxxing slang for the theory that a good smile can substantially raise a person's perceived attractiveness, in some versions enough to offset other facial flaws. Taking 'the smilepill' means accepting that idea, as opposed to the 'blackpill' view that fixed bone structure dominates. [1][3]

People who hold the view use it as a way to look better: they work on how the smile looks (number of teeth shown, width, palate shape, alignment) and on photographing or presenting a smile. One looksmax.org thread argues that an ideal smile shows ten or more upper teeth and links a wide, forward palate to that look, suggesting palate expansion as a route. [3]

The theory is contested inside the community. Other posters argue that smiling helps women's appearance but not men's, that it reads as submissive, or that it makes their own face look worse, and some share before/after photo-rating threads claiming the opposite. [1][2][5][6] No published study is tied to the term itself.

angle.text: Proponents say working on smile width, tooth display and expression raises how attractive a face looks. They test it by comparing smiling and neutral photos and by pursuing dental changes such as palate expansion.

infobox: Smile quality can offset other facial traits
Orthodontics, palate expansion, whitening, expression practice

paras: The word combines 'smile' with the 'pill' metaphor used in the community (bluepill, redpill, blackpill) for worldviews about attractiveness. The smilepill claims that expression and dentition matter more than some bone-structure-focused models allow. [1][3]

In forum posts supporters cite 'smilemoggers', people whose smiles are judged to lift their overall rating, and count visible teeth, with posters describing around 12 teeth in a smile as ideal and 8 or fewer as average. [3][7]
Supporters say a wide palate and forward-set teeth produce a broader smile that photographs better, and that photo-rating experiments comparing smiling and neutral images support the idea. [3][5]

Critics within the community argue that smiling halo effects apply mainly to women, that smiling can look submissive or less masculine on a man, or that it does not flatter their particular face. [1][2]

Described approaches include smile mirror practice, choosing photos with and without a smile, and dental routes such as orthodontics or palate expansion devices discussed as ways to widen the smile. Posters disagree on how effective adult palate expansion is. [3]

lore.intro: The smilepill is debated on looksmax.org, with threads both defending it and calling it overrated. [1][2][3]

claims.claim: A wide 10-12 tooth smile is an attractiveness advantage
claims.believers: Posters say people rated highly tend to show many teeth when smiling and attribute it to a wide, forward palate. [3][7]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this specific framing of tooth count and overall attractiveness.

claims.claim: Smiling helps women but not men
claims.believers: Some posters say smiling made them look less masculine or attracted unwanted treatment, and advise a slight smirk. [1]
claims.experts: No published studies are cited in these threads.

claims.claim: Photo-rating tests show smiling raises ratings
claims.believers: Users post smile versus no-smile results from rating tools as proof the smilepill works. [5]
claims.experts: Informal photo-rating threads are not controlled studies.

claims.claim: Palate expansion can widen the smile
claims.believers: A poster proposes palate expanders to widen the arch and show more teeth. [3]
claims.experts: Orthodontists use expanders mainly in children and adolescents; replies in the thread dispute benefit for adults. [3]
